children: European tariffs are helping the continent's steel industry to offset current high energy prices, boosting earnings, ArcelorMittal said.
Europe's largest steelmaker booked a 34% surge in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a key profit metric, over the third quarter of the year, it said Thursday.
That reflected the "early impacts of the enhanced EU trade measures," the company said.
Amsterdam-listed shares in the Luxembourg-based group gained nearly 6% to 58.26 euros in opening trading.

Under new rules that took effect this summer, imports from outside the European Union and its free-trade partners--above a level set at 18.3 million metric tons--are subject to 50% duties, double a previous rate. Brussels has also put into place a carbon-border adjustment mechanism, known as CBAM, that aims to blunt the competitive edge given to external producers that are not subject to Europe's more stringent caps on carbon emissions.

The move aimed to protect an industry "indispensable to Europe's industrial base" and the green transition toward renewable energy, said Michael Damianos, energy minister for Cyprus, which held the rotating presidency of the European Council at the time.

The measures are "creating a more balanced and sustainable operating environment for the European steel industry, supporting higher capacity utilization and profitability over time," ArcelorMittal Chief Executive Aditya Mittal said. The benefits will be more fully reflected in the company's results from next year on, he said. Flat steel shipments in Europe rose from a quarter earlier, contrary to normal seasonal patterns, ArcelorMittal said.

High energy prices--the result of the conflict in the Middle East that has sent oil-and-gas prices soaring this year--have created a temporary surge in costs for steelmaking, ArcelorMittal said. But lower import volumes have allowed steel prices to adjust to that environment, helping the industry in Europe to earn its cost of capital, the company said.

Higher energy costs are increasingly being reflected in steel pricing, Mittal said. "It is important that this momentum continues, including further action to address the impact of imports in steel-intensive downstream sectors," he said.
The company's upbeat comments offer a boon to the wider European steel industry, analysts at J.P. Morgan wrote following the update.

"Pricing gradually adjusting to align with the industry's higher cost base is a positive read to European steel from a 2027 perspective," the bank said. That could help generate a recovery in companies' bottom lines, despite high costs, the analysts said.
ArcelorMittal said it has brought back all of its European blast furnaces into operation on the back of the protective tariffs.

The company had in previous years been forced to close plants in Germany amid the destabilizing spike in electricity prices that followed the cutting off of Russian gas supplies in the wake of President Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine early in 2022. The sector has also struggled with the impact of tougher emissions rules and weak metals prices.

For the most recent quarter, ArcelorMittal swung to an operating loss of $131 million and a net loss of $391 million, reflecting charges of more than $1 billion that the group booked after being forced to halt operations at its Kryvyi Rih plant in Ukraine following a series of missile attacks that killed workers and did extensive damage to production facilities at the site. Stripping out those charges, net profit rose sharply on year to $868 million.

Looking ahead, the company said it expects earnings to be driven by rising demand and a pipeline of high-return opportunities in attractive markets. Steel shipments in the year's second half should exceed those of the first six months, ArcelorMittal said.
